challenge: TRL scales differ across sources: IEA uses an extended 1-11 scale (TRL 10 = commercial & competitive, TRL 11 = predictable growth) while UK/EU sources use 1-9; ranges like '9-11' are quoted as published rather than converted.

Most flagship UK government studies (Element Energy/Jacobs 2018, Element Energy for CCC 2020, Hy4Heat WP6, ERM NRMM 2023 main text) use qualitative maturity classes or 'first year available' dates instead of numeric TRLs; the numeric TRLs here come disproportionately from IEA (CCUS), Agora/Fraunhofer ISI 2024, TNO factsheets, IEA HPT Annex 58/de Boer, and project-level DESNZ IFS reports.

The IEA ETP Clean Energy Technology Guide is an interactive tool whose per-technology TRLs could not be programmatically accessed; IEA TRLs were taken from the CCUS in Clean Energy Transitions report chapter instead.

No published numeric TRL could be located for: generic waste heat recovery, controls/VSDs, compressed air optimisation, insulation, hydrogen-ready equipment, ammonia as an industrial process-heat fuel, waste-derived fuels, solar thermal SHIP, infrared heating, onsite solar PV, and battery/hydrogen NRMM (numeric TRLs exist in ERM 2023 Appendix 9.8 but were not extractable) - these carry trl: null.

de Boer et al. (2020) TRL statements for the 100-150C and 150-200C bands are phrased as innovation-programme targets as much as status ratings; IEA HPT Annex 58 (2023) corroborates current availability (to ~120C now, ~160C emerging).

Some TRLs are application-specific rather than generic: Essity's TRL 5 (rising to 8) applies to H2 Yankee-hood drying specifically; CalNEXT microwave TRLs vary 3-9 by application; plasma torches are TRL 7-9 as hardware but 'low TRL' in calcination integration.
For HVO and biomethane the numeric TRL rests on commercial-status statements or consultation-response evidence rather than a formal TRL assessment; confidence set to medium.
CCS options are defined generically with 'displaces' empty since they abate rather than displace fuels.

Ceramics UK roadmap technical appendix (which contains sector TRL ratings) returned HTTP 429 and could not be fetched, so several ceramics options carry trl null with status-based evidence instead of published TRL numbers.

Few minerals-sector options have published numeric TRLs; TRL was set to 9 only where commercial deployment is documented (e.g. warm mix asphalt as National Highways default, O.C.O carbonated aggregate UK plants) and left null otherwise per the rules.
Publication years are unavailable for several corporate/NGO web pages (LC3, Holcim, O.C.O, CarbonCure, Origen, ICE, TUC, UKGBC); year is recorded as null with the access date.
No published evidence was found for electric rotary-drum aggregate drying at asphalt plants; that mapping is engineering judgement (prospective, low confidence).
Waste-derived fuel use in high-calcium lime kilns is constrained by product-purity/fuel-contact issues; mapped as prospective on engineering judgement rather than a sector source.
Alkali-activated binder supply chain is fragile in the UK (DB Group, owner of Cemfree, entered administration in 2024), which tempers the 'demonstration/commercial' status of AACM mappings.

Cross-cutting electricity-only processes (homogenisation, forming, setting/handling, cubing/packaging, water pumping) were deliberately left unmapped or given only controls/compressed-air options to keep mapping counts honest.

Search tooling is US-hosted; some UK trade-press sources may be under-represented, though key UK demonstrations (Ribblesdale, Tunstead, HyBrick, Broomfleet, Padeswood, Peak Cluster, mid-Wales hydrogen asphalt) were located directly.

UK BF-BOF applicability is collapsing in real time: Port Talbot's blast furnaces closed in 2024 and Scunthorpe is in special measures, so BF-route options (H2/biochar injection, TGR-BF, HIsarna, BF CCS, Steelanol-type CCU) may have no remaining UK host sites by the time the model is used — the bf_bof process set may need an explicit sunset flag (REF_PORTTALBOT).

Published, citable TRL numbers exist mainly for headline ironmaking and aluminium routes; for auxiliary duties (ladle preheating, sand reclamation, mould drying, dock services) almost no sector-specific decarbonisation literature exists, so many mappings rest on engineering judgement at low confidence.

Several sector options are whole-route replacements (H2-DRI+EAF, HIsarna, MOE, electrowinning, inert anodes, cupola-to-induction) rather than per-process retrofits; mapping them to a single process row (blast_furnace_ironmaking, electrolysis_potlines, melting_holding) understates that they also eliminate upstream processes (coke ovens, sinter, anode plants) — the model may need cross-process linkage.

Grid connection capacity is the recurring binding constraint for the highest-impact options (EAF conversion, induction melting, shore power, induction reheating) but is site-specific and not captured in TRL or applicability ratings.

The UK's single aluminium smelter (Lochaber) is already hydro-powered, so its residual emissions are dominated by anode carbon (process CO2/PFCs); only inert anodes address this, and ELYSIS licensing outside the founders' plants has barely begun.

TRL sources disagree (e.g. Boston Metal self-reports higher readiness than independent assessments; ELYSIS 'commercial-size' cell is still first-of-a-kind); ranges are given and the more conservative published basis cited.
Biochar/biocarbon options share one UK-wide sustainable biomass supply constraint across sinter, BF, EAF and cupola duties — the model should avoid double-counting the same feedstock.

Very few published numeric TRLs exist for food-and-drink-specific technologies; sources use qualitative maturity language (e.g. SWA/Ricardo 'mature'/'least mature'), so trl fields are mostly null with maturity captured in trl_basis and applicability instead

Hydrogen options for distilleries hinge on supply projects (Cromarty, Islay) whose timelines have slipped, so mappings marked demonstration/prospective may regress; HyLaddie demo status should be re-verified before model release
Fuel-vs-feed competition for co-products (draff, pot ale syrup, beet pulp, ABPs) means AD/biomass options carry an opportunity cost not visible in a pure energy mapping
Seasonal/campaign operation (beet sugar ~120-day campaign, malting and creamery seasonality) undermines load factors for capital-intensive options like heat pumps, MVR and CCS
Rural grid connection capacity is the binding constraint for electrification (electrode boilers, MVR, heat-pump kilning) at island distilleries and remote maltings/creameries

Product-quality and food-safety validation (kilned malt flavour, direct-fired combustion contact with malt/singeing, ohmic electrode contact, steam-dried pulp quality) adds time and risk beyond the underlying technology TRL
Two paywalled sources (ScienceDirect abstracts, Taylor & Francis article) could only be verified from abstract/landing pages, and several vendor pages are undated (year set to null)
Brewery and distillery process sets lack an explicit fermentation process, so fermentation_co2_recovery was mapped to packaging (brewery) and site_services (distillery) as the closest hosts

Very few sources publish numeric TRLs; where a source clearly describes deployment stage (lab, pilot, demonstration, commercial) a TRL was assigned using EU TRL definitions and the basis recorded, otherwise TRL is null.

Artificial fibre works have almost no sector-specific decarbonisation literature; mappings rest on process temperatures and engineering judgement (extrusion/drawing already largely electric, chip drying is the main fossil-adjacent duty).

Newspaper print works (coldset) are almost entirely electricity-based with no press dryers, so thermal decarbonisation options barely apply; the material levers are platemaking chemistry, compressed air, and building heat.
Several trade and vendor sources are undated; publication years marked approximate in reference notes rather than invented precisely.
Refinery process heater electrification has no located demonstration or published TRL despite frequent roadmap discussion; treated as prospective with low confidence.
The generic library has no lighting option, so a lab-scoped LED/controls option was added to avoid an empty 'lighting' process for laboratories.

CCS mappings implicitly assume industrial cluster CO2 transport access (HyNet, East Coast); dispersed sites (most paper mills, tanneries, labs) realistically cannot use capture options, which is reflected by omitting CCS from those activities.
Large PDFs (2015 roadmaps, Concawe 19/8, UNIDO reports) were cited at document level without page-level verification of every claimed option discussion; confidence ratings reflect this.
FCC CCS and oxy-FCC evidence is pilot-scale and mostly pre-2020; no operating FCC capture unit was located.
Low-carbon hydrogen options for UK refining and chemicals depend on HyNet/East Coast cluster timing, so 'demonstration' applicability may overstate near-term availability for sites outside clusters.

Few sources publish numeric TRLs for these technologies; TRLs given are inferred from published deployment/demonstration status rather than formal TRL assessments, and set to null only where even deployment-status evidence was lacking.

Grid connection capacity and cost at rural quarry, AD and treatment sites is the binding constraint for nearly every electrification option (static plant, plug-in mobile crushing, charging, MVR), but is site-specific and not captured in the option-level TRL.

Evidence for trolley assist, IPCC and hydrogen haul trucks comes from large international mines; transfer to UK quarry scale (smaller trucks, shorter site lives) is uncertain, so applicability was rated prospective/speculative despite high overseas maturity.
Minewater heat recovery is primarily a heat-export/revenue option displacing offtakers' gas, not the site's own fuel; the model may need a convention for crediting exported heat.

AD options interact strongly: CHP heat integration, biogas upgrading and heat-pump digester heating are partly mutually exclusive strategies, so mappings should be treated as alternatives, not additive.
UK deep coal mining has ceased and surface coal mining is nearly ended, so 'Mineral Production - Coal' mappings (especially VAM abatement) apply mainly to legacy or closure operations.

MPA roadmap detail covers cement manufacture far more than quarrying itself, so several quarry mobile-plant mappings rest on OEM/trade-press evidence or engineering judgement rather than sector roadmap provenance.
The salt/brine provenance (PBL) is Dutch; no UK-specific published decarbonisation study for vacuum salt production was located.

Published TRLs rarely exist for building-services and workshop efficiency measures (LED, destratification, fabric, inverter welders, regen drives); TRLs left null and readiness expressed via the applicability field instead

The best public paint-shop measure compendium (ENERGY STAR vehicle assembly guide, LBNL 2008) is US-focused and dated; UK OEM disclosures on low-bake/UV/EB body coatings are proprietary, so readiness there is judged from DOE workshop and trade sources
Several Carbon Trust and vendor web guides are undated; reference years are approximate and flagged in reference notes

'Factory', 'Works' and 'Industrial NEC' activities are highly heterogeneous, so process_heating and steam mappings assume generic low/medium-temperature light-manufacturing duties; site-level screening should confirm temperature bands before applying heat pump options
Hydrogen options (h2_boiler, h2_kiln_furnace_burner) are mapped as prospective because UK industrial hydrogen supply outside cluster areas does not yet exist for dispersed light-manufacturing sites

The electricity-to-gas price ratio (spark spread) is the binding economic constraint on all commercial-readiness electrification mappings, especially electrode boilers, electric ovens and electric radiant space heating
EV fleet charging is an enabler whose emissions savings accrue to vehicle fleets, which may sit outside the site process model's system boundary
